rewrites.summary:
For a transgender visitor the protection gap is the deciding fact: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been outlawed since 2013 and private adult same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1994. For a same-sex couple travelling together the available status is partnership, not marriage: marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act, making this the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality, and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld the traditional-marriage definition, so no marriage route is open to same-sex partners.

Practical safety is the weaker element: church influence in local politics is significant — when a gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007, religious objections had to be countered by the premier's defence — and the tourism economy has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity, suggesting that visible same-sex couples can meet organised religious hostility in a visitor-facing setting.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Statutory and litigation flux frames this visitor-relevant status: marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act applying to both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making this the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality, and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld the restored traditional-marriage definition. The record carries no claims about parent-country policy turbulence or neighbouring-jurisdiction comparisons on these questions, so the reversal's uniqueness is the only comparative frame the sources support.
rewrites.localsOnly: For residents the 1994 decriminalisation itself divided the community: the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, and the debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and religious groups led by the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. The 2013 human-rights amendment outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and the 2018 Domestic Partnership Act governing family status for same-sex and heterosexual couples alike are the resident-facing legal landmarks.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary. No source covers border screening or identity-document practice for transgender visitors, so that element of the visitor picture is unverifiable; nothing in the record documents how the 2013 discrimination ban is enforced in practice.

blindSourceSummaries: A 2018 news report: the governor of the state/province gave assent to a 2017 domestic-partnership statute replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, the change that made this the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality — evidence for the partnerships-not-marriage status facing visiting same-sex couples.

A news report on the social climate: local churches protested a gay-charity cruise planning to dock at the state/province on religious grounds, organised hostility toward visible same-sex couples in a visitor-facing setting that the premier had to defend against.

A 2013 news report: the elected local legislature passed a human-rights amendment act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination), while same-sex marriage was not then permitted — the sexual-orientation protection that leaves transgender visitors without gender-identity-specific protection.

A 1994 news report: the elected local legislature voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two criminal-code sections, with religious groups staging marches against the change — the decriminalisation baseline for private adult same-sex conduct.
rewrites.notes: Split from merged summary per rule 6: trans-visitor protection gap and same-sex partner-travel status to summary (visitor lens), reversal/litigation flux to tangentialFactors, resident-facing decriminalisation debate and local legal landmarks to localsOnly, screening/enforcement gaps to outOfScopeNotes. Blind mirrors derived per rule 7/7e: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council -> national court, Domestic Partnership Act -> statute, House of Assembly/Senate -> the elected local legislature, Christian Coalition -> religious groups, island/United Kingdom/Territory handled via omit or state/province + parent nation; no proper names, demonyms, or slogans in blind text.
